title: The tutor loop
use: Any new skill or subject. Turns a chat into an active tutor instead of a lecture.
text: You are my tutor for [SUBJECT]. I know [WHAT YOU KNOW] but not [WHAT YOU DON'T]. Explain one concept at a time in plain language, then give me a tiny exercise to check I understood. Wait for my answer before continuing. If I'm wrong, explain differently — don't repeat the same words.

title: Explain it 5 ways
use: When something just won't click after three tutorials.
text: Explain [CONCEPT] to me five different ways: 1) like I'm 12, 2) with a cooking analogy, 3) with a sports analogy, 4) as its history (why it exists), 5) in one perfect sentence. Then tell me which explanation most beginners should use.

title: Quiz me hard
use: Exam prep. Recall beats re-reading — this forces recall.
text: Quiz me on [TOPIC]. One question at a time, increasing difficulty. After each answer: correct it if wrong, explain why the right answer is right, then ask the next. 10 questions total, then give me a score and my 2 weakest areas.

title: The Feynman check
use: Testing whether you actually understand something (the best study move there is).
text: I'll explain [TOPIC] in my own words below. Find every gap, error, or hand-wave in my explanation. Be specific about what I glossed over, then ask me the one question that would expose my weakest point.

title: The scolding project planner
use: Before starting any project. Cuts scope before you waste weekends.
text: I want to build [PROJECT]. Assume I'm a beginner with [X HOURS] per week. Give me: 1) the smallest version that is still genuinely worth shipping, 2) everything I should cut from my idea for version 1, 3) the first 30-minute task. Be ruthless about cutting.

title: Explain this code line by line
use: Reading real code — the fastest way to level up.
text: Explain this code to a beginner, line by line. Then: 1) what it does overall, 2) the three concepts a beginner must understand to have written it themselves, 3) one small change I could make and what it would do. CODE: [PASTE]

title: The error whisperer
use: When something breaks. Gets you a diagnosis, not a panic.
text: I got this error: [PASTE ERROR + what you were doing]. Explain: 1) what the error actually means in plain words, 2) the 3 most likely causes ranked, 3) how I check which one it is, 4) the fix for each. Don't rewrite all my code — diagnose first.

title: Design my automation
text: I want to automate [BORING TASK], which I do [HOW OFTEN]. It involves [TOOLS/APPS]. Design the simplest automation that would work, step by step: trigger → steps → output. Flag anything that needs a human in the loop, and tell me honestly if a 5-minute manual habit would beat automating it.

title: Critique my prompt
use: The meta-move: improve the thing that improves everything else.
text: Here is a prompt I keep using: [PROMPT]. Critique it: 1) what information I'm forcing the AI to guess, 2) what format I forgot to specify, 3) rewrite it twice — once for better output, once shorter. Then tell me the one habit that would improve ALL my future prompts.

title: Critique, don't rewrite
use: Improving writing while keeping YOUR voice.
text: Critique this draft. Do NOT rewrite it. List: 1) sentences that are unclear, 2) words that sound corporate or lazy, 3) what's missing that a reader would wonder about, 4) the single weakest paragraph and why. DRAFT: [PASTE]

title: The hook factory
use: Video intros, post openings, first lines that stop the scroll.
text: My content is about [TOPIC] for [AUDIENCE]. Write 10 opening lines that make someone stop scrolling: 5 curiosity-based, 3 mistake/warning-based, 2 bold-claim-based. Each under 12 words. Then tell me which one you'd bet on and why.

title: Translate to beginner
use: When your draft accidentally sounds like a textbook.
text: Rewrite this for a total beginner: [DRAFT]. Rules: no jargon without a one-line explanation, sentences under 20 words, one idea per paragraph, keep my point but make it land in the first 2 sentences.

title: The decision table
use: Choosing between tools, languages, laptops, options of any kind.
text: I'm choosing between [OPTION A] and [OPTION B] for [USE CASE]. My priorities in order: [PRIORITIES]. Build a decision table, score both honestly, declare a winner for MY case — and then steel-man the losing option: what would have to be true for it to be the right choice?

title: The weekly review
use: End of week — 10 minutes that make next week actually different.
text: Here is what I did this week: [BRAIN DUMP]. Ask me 5 sharp questions about it, one at a time, to figure out: 1) what actually moved me forward, 2) what was fake work, 3) the one thing to do more of next week and the one thing to stop. End with a 3-item plan for next week.

title: Rubber duck, upgraded
use: Stuck on ANY problem — code, plan, essay, decision.
text: Act as my rubber duck. I'll explain my problem and my current approach. Your job: ask me one question at a time, each designed to expose what I haven't thought about. Do not give me the answer until I say 'ok solve it' — make me find it first.
